Ransomware Attack Disrupts Curacao Oil & Gas Producers, Crippling Exports

A major ransomware attack has struck the information technology systems of several leading oil and gas producers in Curacao, forcing the suspension of critical operations and halting the export of petroleum products from the island. The cyber incident, which began early Tuesday morning, continues to unfold, with companies racing to contain the impact and restore their systems.

The affected firms, including Isla Energy Group and Caribbean Hydrocarbons Ltd, confirmed in statements that the attack had compromised key IT infrastructure supporting their refining and export logistics. “We detected unauthorized access to our operational network and immediately initiated shutdown protocols to protect our assets,” said Isla Energy Group’s Chief Executive, Ricardo Alvarez. “At this time, we are unable to safely process or ship crude and refined products.”

Local authorities estimate that the disruption has idled at least 70% of Curacao’s daily oil export capacity, which averages 160,000 barrels per day. The island, situated off the coast of Venezuela, is a vital hub for transshipment and refining in the southern Caribbean region.

“Our technical teams are working around the clock in coordination with international cybersecurity experts,” said Alicia Martina, Curacao’s Minister for Economic Development. “We cannot yet provide a timeline for the resumption of full operations, but our priority is to ensure the integrity of our critical infrastructure.”

Industry experts warn that the longer the outage persists, the greater the risk of contractual penalties, supply shortages, and revenue losses for the companies involved. “Cybersecurity vulnerabilities in the energy sector have long been a concern,” observed Juan de la Paz, analyst at the Caribbean Energy Institute. “This incident underscores how dependent oil and gas producers are on digital infrastructure for everything from safety controls to export scheduling.”

The Curacao Oil Workers Union has called for greater transparency from company management. “Employees are anxious about both safety and job security,” said union president, Miriam van Dijk. “We want assurances that systems will be restored safely and that this incident will not lead to layoffs.”

The Curacao Oil & Gas Producers Association urged patience from international trading partners. “We are in direct contact with our clients and are doing everything possible to minimize disruptions,” said the association in a statement released Wednesday afternoon.

As of press time, no group has claimed responsibility for the ransomware attack, and authorities have not disclosed whether any ransom demands have been received. The situation remains fluid, with local officials warning that the full extent of the damage may not be clear for several days.
